items.title: Global temperature, 1880–2025 (from NASA data)
items.description: Each year from 1880 to 2025 becomes one note, taken from NASA's measured global temperature record. NASA's map animation of the same record plays in step above a chart with one colored stripe per year (blue for cooler than the 1951–1980 average, red for warmer) and a line tracing the values.
items.summary: For the first sixty years the notes stay low and wander. From about 1980 they climb steadily, and the last decade holds the highest notes of the whole piece. The warmest year in the record is 2024.

keyMoments.text: 1880: the record begins, slightly below the 1951–1980 average.
1909: the coldest year in the record, about 0.48 °C below the average. This is the lowest note.
1944: a warm peak in the 1940s, about 0.20 °C above the average.
1964: a brief dip to about 0.20 °C below the average.
1980: the steady climb begins. Most notes from here are higher than the ones before.
1998: a sharp jump to about 0.61 °C above the average during a strong El Niño.
2016: the first year more than 1 °C above the average.
2024: the warmest year in the record, about 1.28 °C above the average. This is the highest note.

companion.label: NASA's map animation of the same data (visualization 5603)

visual.caption: a chart with one stripe per year. Blue is cooler than the 1951–1980 average and red is warmer; the line and the label show the same values, so nothing depends on color alone.

pitch.explain: Warmer year, higher note. Cooler year, lower note.
pitch.bounds: 220–880 Hz (A3 to A5), snapped to a five-note scale

loudness.explain: As the long-term average rises, the sound gets gently louder.
loudness.bounds: Always between half and full level, under a fixed ceiling

timbre.explain: Cooler years sound soft and mellow. Warmer years sound brighter and sharper.
timbre.bounds: Filter opens from 1.5× to 9× the note's pitch

pan.explain: The sound travels from your left ear (1880) to your right ear (2025).

texture.explain: A soft, low rush of air appears only when one year is very different from the year before.
texture.bounds: Very quiet, and silent for small changes

source.name: GISS Surface Temperature Analysis (GISTEMP v4), NASA Goddard Institute for Space Studies
source.attribution: GISTEMP Team, 2026: GISS Surface Temperature Analysis (GISTEMP), version 4. NASA Goddard Institute for Space Studies.
source.license: NASA data, free to reuse with credit. See the GISTEMP page for citation guidance.
source.related: Shown as a map animation in NASA SVS visualization 5603, https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/5603/

limitations: The sound follows the global yearly average only. It says nothing about where on Earth the warming is.
Notes are snapped to a musical scale, so two years with slightly different values can share a note. Switch the pitch curve to Linear or Logarithmic to hear the unsnapped values.
Values were read from the NASA GISS file on 15 November 2026. NASA revises recent years slightly over time; run tools/update_data.py to refresh them.

items.title: Arctic temperature, 1880–2025 (from NASA data)
items.description: Each year from 1880 to 2025 becomes one note, taken from NASA's temperature record for the Arctic, the region north of 64° latitude. Values are compared with the 1951–1980 average. The chart shows one colored stripe per year with a line tracing the values.
items.summary: The Arctic swings far more from year to year than the planet as a whole, so the notes leap around. There is a cold stretch in the 1880s, a warm spell around 1940, a cooler dip in the 1960s, and then a steep climb from the 1990s. Over the last ten years the Arctic averaged about 2.6 °C above its 1951–1980 level, roughly two and a half times the global figure of about 1.0 °C.

keyMoments.text: 1887: the coldest year in the record, about 1.73 °C below the average. This is the lowest note.
1938: the peak of an early warm spell, about 1.52 °C above the average.
1966: a cold dip, about 0.76 °C below the average.
1992: the last year colder than the 1951–1980 average.
2005: the first year at least 2 °C above the average.
2016: the warmest year in the record, about 3.23 °C above the average. This is the highest note.
2025: the record ends at about 2.93 °C above the average, the second-warmest year.

visual.caption: A chart with one stripe per year. Blue is cooler than the 1951–1980 average and red is warmer; the line and the label show the same values, so nothing depends on color alone.

pitch.drivenBy: Arctic temperature anomaly for the year
pitch.explain: Warmer year, higher note. Cooler year, lower note.
pitch.bounds: 220–880 Hz (A3 to A5), snapped to a five-note scale

loudness.explain: As the long-term average rises, the sound gets gently louder.
loudness.bounds: Always between half and full level, under a fixed ceiling

timbre.drivenBy: Arctic temperature anomaly for the year
timbre.explain: Cooler years sound soft and mellow. Warmer years sound brighter and sharper.
timbre.bounds: Filter opens from 1.5× to 9× the note's pitch

pan.explain: The sound travels from your left ear (1880) to your right ear (2025).

texture.explain: A soft, low rush of air appears only when one year is very different from the year before.
texture.bounds: Very quiet, and silent for small changes

source.name: GISS Surface Temperature Analysis (GISTEMP v4), zonal annual means, NASA Goddard Institute for Space Studies
source.attribution: GISTEMP Team, 2026: GISS Surface Temperature Analysis (GISTEMP), version 4. NASA Goddard Institute for Space Studies.
source.license: NASA data, free to reuse with credit. See the GISTEMP page for citation guidance.

limitations: The pitch range is fitted to the Arctic's own record, which spans almost 5 °C. The same note here and in the global temperature item does not mean the same temperature. Compare the numbers, not the notes.
Notes are snapped to a musical scale. Switch the pitch curve to Linear or Logarithmic to hear the unsnapped values.
Early Arctic values rest on few weather stations and are less certain than recent ones.

items.title: Carbon dioxide in the air, 1959–2025 (from NOAA data)
items.description: Each year from 1959 to 2025 becomes one note, taken from the yearly average amount of carbon dioxide in the air measured at Mauna Loa Observatory in Hawaii, in parts per million. The chart shows one colored stripe per year with a line tracing the values.
items.summary: The notes only ever go up. Carbon dioxide rises every single year in the record, from about 316 parts per million in 1959 to about 427 in 2025. The climb also gets steeper: about 0.9 parts per million a year in the 1960s, and about 2.6 a year over the last ten years. A brighter, sharper tone marks the years with the biggest jumps.

keyMoments.text: 1959: the first full year of measurements, about 316 parts per million. This is the lowest note.
1988: carbon dioxide passes 350 parts per million.
2015: carbon dioxide passes 400 parts per million.
2023: carbon dioxide passes 420 parts per million.
2024: the largest one-year rise in the record, about 3.5 parts per million.
2025: about 427 parts per million, the highest in the record. This is the highest note.

visual.caption: A chart with one stripe per year. Stripes run from blue for the lowest values in the record to red for the highest; the line and the label show the same values, so nothing depends on color alone.

pitch.bounds: 220–880 Hz (A3 to A5), snapped to a five-note scale

loudness.explain: As the long-term level rises, the sound gets gently louder.
loudness.bounds: Always between half and full level, under a fixed ceiling

timbre.drivenBy: Size of the rise since the previous year
timbre.explain: A bigger one-year rise sounds brighter and sharper. A smaller rise sounds mellow.
timbre.bounds: Filter opens from 1.5× to 9× the note's pitch

pan.explain: The sound travels from your left ear (1959) to your right ear (2025).

source.name: Trends in Atmospheric Carbon Dioxide, Mauna Loa Observatory, NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory
source.attribution: NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory and Scripps Institution of Oceanography.
source.license: NOAA data, freely available with credit to NOAA GML.
source.related: This record is from NOAA, not NASA. NASA shows the same measurements on its climate pages.

limitations: These are yearly averages from one mountain-top station. They track the global trend closely but leave out the seasonal rise and fall within each year.
Notes are snapped to a musical scale, so two neighbouring years can share a note even though the value rose. Switch the pitch curve to Linear or Logarithmic to hear every rise.

items.title: Arctic sea ice in September, 1979–2026 (from satellite data)
items.description: Each year from 1979 to 2026 becomes one note, taken from the satellite record of how much of the Arctic Ocean is covered by sea ice in September, the month when the ice is at its smallest. Values are in millions of square kilometres. The chart shows one colored stripe per year with a line tracing the values.
items.summary: Here a falling note means less ice. The notes start high and drift down for twenty years, drop sharply in 2007, and hit the lowest note in 2012. Since then they have stayed low without falling further. September ice averaged about 7.2 million square kilometres in the first ten years of the record and about 4.6 million in the last ten, a loss of more than a third.

keyMoments.text: 1980: the most September ice in the record, about 7.67 million square kilometres. This is the highest note.
1996: the last year close to the early levels, about 7.58 million square kilometres.
2003: the last September with more than 6 million square kilometres of ice.
2007: a sharp drop to about 4.27 million square kilometres.
2012: the least September ice in the record, about 3.57 million square kilometres. This is the lowest note.
2020: the second-lowest year, about 4.00 million square kilometres.
2026: the record ends at about 4.81 million square kilometres.

visual.caption: A chart with one stripe per year. Blue stripes are years with more ice and red stripes are years with less; the line and the label show the same values, so nothing depends on color alone.

pitch.drivenBy: September sea ice extent for the year
pitch.explain: More ice, higher note. Less ice, lower note.
pitch.bounds: 220–880 Hz (A3 to A5), snapped to a five-note scale

loudness.explain: Loudness stays the same throughout, so quiet is never mistaken for less ice.
loudness.bounds: Fixed level, under a fixed ceiling

timbre.drivenBy: September sea ice extent for the year
timbre.explain: Years with more ice sound brighter. Years with less ice sound duller and more muffled.
timbre.bounds: Filter opens from 1.5× to 9× the note's pitch

pan.explain: The sound travels from your left ear (1979) to your right ear (2026).

texture.explain: A soft, low rush of air appears only when one year is very different from the year before, as in 2007.
texture.bounds: Very quiet, and silent for small changes

source.name: Sea Ice Index (dataset G02135), National Snow and Ice Data Center
source.attribution: National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC), Boulder, Colorado USA.
source.license: Freely available with credit to NSIDC. See the dataset page for the full citation.
source.related: This record is from NSIDC, a data center supported by NASA and NOAA. It is built from satellite microwave measurements.

limitations: Extent counts ocean area with at least 15% ice cover. It says nothing about how thick the ice is, and thickness has also declined.
Only September is included, so the yearly freeze and melt cycle is not heard.
Notes are snapped to a musical scale. Switch the pitch curve to Linear or Logarithmic to hear the unsnapped values.

items.title: Global temperature map, by color (from NASA frames)
items.description: NASA's animated world map of temperature anomalies from 1880 to 2025. Blues mark places cooler than the 1951–1980 average and reds mark places warmer. Here the sound is computed live from the colors of each video frame, not from the temperature numbers.
items.summary: Early in the animation the map is a patchwork of pale blues and reds. Toward the end, red spreads across almost the whole map, most strongly over the Arctic and the northern continents.

pitch.drivenBy: Balance of warm colors against cool colors in the frame
pitch.explain: More red than blue on screen, higher note. More blue than red, lower note.
pitch.bounds: 220–880 Hz (A3 to A5), snapped to a five-note scale

density.drivenBy: Share of the frame covered by the selected color
density.explain: The more of the picture the selected color covers, the faster the notes repeat.
density.bounds: From one note every two seconds up to six notes a second

loudness.explain: A brighter picture sounds a little louder.
loudness.bounds: Always under a fixed ceiling, with a volume control

timbre.drivenBy: Share of the frame covered by the selected color
timbre.explain: More of the selected color makes the tone brighter.
timbre.bounds: Filter opens from 1.5× to 9× the note's pitch

pan.drivenBy: Where the selected color sits, left to right
pan.explain: If the selected color is mostly on the left of the picture, the sound moves left, and the same for the right.

texture.drivenBy: How much the picture changed since the last sample
texture.explain: A soft, low rush of air appears only when the picture is changing quickly. Most of the time it is silent.
texture.bounds: Very quiet, and silent for small changes

source.name: Global Temperature Anomalies from 1880 to 2025, NASA Scientific Visualization Studio (visualization 5603)
source.attribution: NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio. Scientific consulting by Gavin A. Schmidt (NASA/GSFC GISS). Visualizations by Mark SubbaRao (NASA/GSFC).
source.license: NASA media. Credit NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio and follow NASA's media usage guidelines.

limitations: This sound is derived from image features. Color on screen is a picture of the data, not the measurement itself, so legends, labels and the map outline also affect the sound.
For the measured values, listen to the 'from NASA data' item, which uses the GISTEMP numbers behind this map.
The year shown on screen is not read by the app. The animation runs from 1880 to 2025 at a steady pace over one minute.

items.title: Spread of the Dixie Fire, 2021 (from NASA frames)
items.description: NASA's animation of the Dixie Fire in California from 14 July to 22 October 2021, updated every 12 hours from satellite fire detections. Yellow lines mark recent fire fronts (the newest is brightest), red dots mark active fire detections, and grey shading shows the total area burned. A graph on screen tracks the cumulative burned area. The sound is computed live from the colors of each frame.
items.summary: The fire begins as a small patch in mid-July. Through late July and early August the grey burned area spreads quickly across the map while the view pulls back to keep it in frame. In mid-August active fire is burning along the northern and eastern edges. From September the red detections become few, and by 30 September none are visible; the graph of burned area has levelled off. The final frame overlays the outlines of all the earlier fire fronts.

pitch.drivenBy: Share of the frame showing vivid red (active fire detections)
pitch.explain: More active fire on screen, higher note. No active fire, the lowest note.
pitch.bounds: 220–880 Hz (A3 to A5), snapped to a five-note scale

density.drivenBy: How much the picture changed since the last sample
density.explain: When the burned area is growing quickly the notes come faster. When the fire stalls they slow down.
density.bounds: From one note every two seconds up to six notes a second

loudness.explain: A brighter picture sounds a little louder.
loudness.bounds: Always under a fixed ceiling, with a volume control

timbre.drivenBy: Share of the frame showing vivid red
timbre.explain: More active fire makes the tone brighter and sharper.
timbre.bounds: Filter opens from 1.5× to 9× the note's pitch

pan.drivenBy: Where the vivid red sits, left to right
pan.explain: If the active fire is mostly on the left of the map, the sound moves left, and the same for the right.

texture.drivenBy: How much the picture changed since the last sample
texture.explain: A soft, low rush of air appears only when the picture is changing quickly. Most of the time it is silent.
texture.bounds: Very quiet, and silent for small changes

source.name: Spread of the Dixie Fire - 2021, NASA Scientific Visualization Studio (visualization 4993)
source.license: NASA media. Credit NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio and follow NASA's media usage guidelines.
source.related: Part of the Earth Information Center gallery, https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/gallery/earth-information-center/

The camera pulls back during the first weeks, which also changes the picture and so adds to the rhythm there.
The on-screen graph and labels are part of the picture and can affect the sound.
This is the 4x-speed version of NASA's animation.

items.title: Ocean surface currents and temperature, 2007–2008 (from NASA frames)
items.description: NASA's animation of global sea surface currents from 25 March 2007 to 3 March 2008. The flow lines are colored by sea surface temperature: blue for 0 °C, through green and yellow, to red for 32 °C. The sound is computed live from the colors of each frame.
items.summary: A flat map of the world's oceans, with land in grey. Swirling flow lines cover the water: red and orange along the tropics where the sea is warmest, green and yellow at middle latitudes, and blue near the poles. Over the year the pattern changes gently. The warm band strengthens and weakens, and the reddest water shifts between the western Pacific, the Indian Ocean and the tropical Atlantic.

pitch.explain: More warm-colored water on screen, higher note. More cool-colored water, lower note.
pitch.bounds: 220–880 Hz (A3 to A5), snapped to a five-note scale

density.drivenBy: Share of the frame showing vivid red (the warmest water)
density.explain: The more of the very warmest water on screen, the faster the notes repeat.
density.bounds: From one note every two seconds up to six notes a second

loudness.explain: A brighter picture sounds a little louder.
loudness.bounds: Always under a fixed ceiling, with a volume control

timbre.drivenBy: Share of the frame showing vivid red (the warmest water)
timbre.explain: More of the warmest water makes the tone brighter.
timbre.bounds: Filter opens from 1.5× to 9× the note's pitch

pan.drivenBy: Where the vivid red sits, left to right
pan.explain: If the warmest water is mostly on the left of the map, the sound moves left, and the same for the right.

texture.drivenBy: How much the picture changed since the last sample
texture.explain: A soft, low rush of air appears only when the picture is changing quickly. Most of the time it is silent.

The whole-ocean picture changes only a little over the year, so the app stretches those small changes to make them audible. The size of a change in the sound is not the size of the change in the ocean.

items.title: Lightning seen from the Space Station, 2017–2023 (from NASA frames)
items.description: NASA's animation of lightning detected by the Lightning Imaging Sensor on the International Space Station from January 2017 through July 2023. A moving 10-day window brings out the seasonal pattern. The sound is computed live from the colors of each frame.
items.summary: The animation begins on 1 March 2017, following the Space Station's track across a dark Earth as the first flashes appear as yellow dots. It then shows the whole globe slowly turning while a 10-day window moves through the years to 2023. Yellow dots gather thickly over land in the tropics, especially central Africa, South America and south-east Asia, and thin out over the open ocean. The clusters shift north and south with the seasons.

pitch.explain: More lightning on screen, higher note.

density.explain: More lightning on screen, faster notes.

loudness.bounds: Always under a fixed ceiling, with a volume control

timbre.explain: More lightning makes the tone brighter.
timbre.bounds: Filter opens from 1.5× to 9× the note's pitch

The globe turns during the animation, so lightning-rich regions come into view and leave it. Some of the rise and fall you hear is the turning globe, not a change in lightning.
The sensor sees only the part of Earth beneath the Space Station's orbit, so high latitudes are not covered.
